newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Medeva hungry for acquisitions.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Medeva hungry for acquisitions.

text.p: British drugs group Medeva Plc suggested on Friday that further product and company acquisitions could be in store to make up for any potential shortfall in sales of its lead product, hyperactivity drug Methylphenidate.

In an interview with Reuters, chief executive Bill Bogie played down analysts' fears that the company could face 18 months of dull earnings in 1998 and 1999 before new products can make up for any decline in Methylphenidate sales.

Medeva's generic version of the drug, used principally to counter attention deficit disorder in children and young adults, currently dominates the key U.S. market and has been its main, sometimes exclusive, source of profits. However, this position is expected to slip as the market reaches saturation and new generic competitors are allowed in to the strictly-controlled supply system.

Bogie declined to give forecasts for Methylphenidate sales, but he said, "You can't look at the palette as it is and say those are the colours that are going to be on the painting. Medeva is about acquisitions."

Last year Medeva's unique strategy of building an international pharmaceutical company by buying existing businesses and products and grafting on drugs in late-stage development moved up several notches with the $400 million acquisition of a package of U.S. and French assets from Rhone Poulenc Rorer Inc.
Bogie said that acquisition, Medeva's biggest, had "gone without a hiccough. That should give confidence to us and the City if we were to do another one of a similar size."

The U.S. assets, including manufacturing facilities, offices and a hotch-potch of products, meant that further acquisitions in the U.S. would be very profitable given the existence of a unified management and sales force.
The company wants to exploit its excess manufacturing capacity by producing drugs under license for others.
Medeva believes there are other, similar opportunities in the U.S. to the RPR deal, but Bogie said further purchases had to provide long-term earnings opportunities.

Germany also remains high on Medeva's shopping list. Bogie told Reuters the group came close to clinching an acquisition there last year, but he noted that suitable companies were thin on the ground. Medeva has gradually filled gaps elsewhere in its European infrastructure through the RPR deal in France and the acquisition of a package of products and a sales team from Glaxo Wellcome Plc in Spain. It also has a strong position in Switzerland.
But Bogie said it had cooled on buying a business in Italy where the government's volatile attitude towards the drugs industry has created a climate of uncertainty.

Investors can also expect further activity on the product-acquisition front. As well as adding to its five core areas of respiratory, gastro-intestinal and central nervous system drugs plus hospital products and vaccines, Bogie is clearly keen to add opportunities in niche areas where Medeva's sales team doesn't have to compete head-on with the industry's big boys.

Bogie believes the success of Hepagene, a vaccination against the deadly Hepatitis B virus which has been shown to work on people who do not respond to existing vaccinations, will be a major boost to Medeva's vaccine business.

Medeva has already tied up a deal with tiny UK biotech group Peptide Therapeutics Plc to research into replacing injections against illnesses like typhoid, influenza and tetanus with nasal sprays or capsules. But the biggest boost for the group would be news that Hepagene, which is to be filed with authorities in Europe and the U.S. next year, could also act as a treatment for the condition, which kills two million people a year. Trial results on this much more significant use of the drug are due in September.
